fixes.explanation: Bronze it is. Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, wore a bronze helmet, a bronze coat of mail and bronze armor on his legs, and he carried a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders (1 Samuel 17:5-6). That's a lot of bronze. I can't even get my oven mitts to match.
Gold isn't the answer, friend. The text names bronze for his helmet, his coat of mail, his leg armor and his javelin (1 Samuel 17:5-6). Gold is a fancy guess, but bronze is what the text gives.

That's exactly what he asks. Goliath shouts, "Choose one of your men and have him come down against me." It's one man against one man. Then he lays out the stakes: the loser's side becomes the servants of the winner's side (1 Samuel 17:8-9).
He asks for one man, not the whole army. His words were, "Choose one of your men and have him come down against me." So it's a single man he wants sent down, not a crowd (1 Samuel 17:8).

That's what the text says. When Saul, king of Israel, and all the Israelites heard the Philistine's words, they were dismayed and greatly afraid (1 Samuel 17:11). That's the whole camp, from the king on down. Goliath's challenge reached everybody.
Calm would have been nice, friend. But the text says Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid (1 Samuel 17:11). So calm isn't the word. Dismayed and greatly afraid is.

Youngest it is. Jesse, an old man from Bethlehem, had eight sons, and the text says David was the youngest (1 Samuel 17:12-14). His three oldest brothers had followed Saul. David was last in line, and I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about being at the back.

Not fifth. Jesse had eight sons, and the text says David was the youngest (1 Samuel 17:12-14). Fifth would put him somewhere in the middle, but the text puts him at the very end of the line. That's behind Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah and all the rest.

Seven days would have been bad enough, but it went way longer. The text says Goliath came forward every morning and evening for forty days (1 Samuel 17:16). That's morning and evening, day after day. Forty days is a long time to keep showing up.

It was much longer than three. The text says, "For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand." (1 Samuel 17:16). That's forty days of morning and evening appearances.

Nobody's holding the line, friend. The text says when all the men of Israel saw Goliath, they fled from him in great fear (1 Samuel 17:24). Fleeing is the opposite of standing still. That's what the text tells us they did.

That's the offer going around camp. The men of Israel said the king would give great riches to the man who kills Goliath, and he would give him his daughter in marriage (1 Samuel 17:25). That's a very big prize.

The text doesn't mention a seat at the head of the army. What the men of Israel said was that the king would give great riches and his daughter in marriage (1 Samuel 17:25). That seat isn't part of the offer they describe.

False is right. When Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him speaking to the men, his anger burned against David. He said, "I know your pride and wickedness of heart—you have come down to see the battle!" David answered, "What have I done now?" (1 Samuel 17:28-29).

He sure does. David tells Saul, "Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!" (1 Samuel 17:32). Quite a day for a shepherd who was sent with supplies for his brothers (1 Samuel 17:17-18).
Not that one. David tells Saul, "Your servant will go and fight him!" (1 Samuel 17:32). He offers to go out and fight the Philistine himself. Bringing more men isn't part of his offer.

It doesn't work out that way. David strapped his sword over the tunic and tried to walk, but he told Saul, "I cannot walk in these…" and "I am not accustomed to them." So David took them off (1 Samuel 17:39). The text says he wasn't used to the gear.
The text gives the reason right away. When Goliath looked at David, "…he despised him because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome." (1 Samuel 17:42). He looked, he saw David, and he despised him.

True. Goliath had just asked if he was a dog that David came at him with sticks (1 Samuel 17:43). Then he calls to David, "Come here," and says, "…and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field!" (1 Samuel 17:44). That's the threat he makes.

That's what David says. "This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand… Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel." (1 Samuel 17:46). What he says the world will know is about God, not about David.

That's David's reason. He says, "…it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands." He says it to all those assembled there (1 Samuel 17:47). The reason he gives is that the battle belongs to the LORD.

Forehead. David "…took out a stone, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead." Then the stone sank into his forehead, and Goliath fell facedown on the ground (1 Samuel 17:49). The text says David did it with a sling and a stone (1 Samuel 17:50). One stone, one shot.

False, and you got it. "…David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him." There was no sword in his hand when it happened. The sword only came after, when David pulled Goliath's own sword from its sheath (1 Samuel 17:51).
It's false, friend. The text says, "When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran." (1 Samuel 17:51). No second champion steps up. They ran instead.
Jericho isn't in this chase. The men of Israel and Judah pursued the Philistines "…to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron." (1 Samuel 17:52). That's where the pursuit reached.
Jesse. Saul asks, "Whose son are you, young man?" and David answers, "I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem…" (1 Samuel 17:58). That's the name David gives.
